How wickets fall in T20I & ODI cricket

Research title

Association of Bowling Characteristics and Shot Type with the Mode and Fielding Location of Wicket Taking Dismissals in T20 International and One Day International (ODI) Cricket

How bowling length, line, bowler type, variation and the batter's stroke decide where a catch is taken and whether a stump-attacking ball ends LBW or Bowled. Every number is estimated from, or recomputed from, the study datasets.

Author
E. A. P. D. Edirisinghe S/20/364
Supervisor
Prof. Y. P. R. D. Yapa
Institution
Department of Statistics and Computer Science Faculty of Science
University of Peradeniya
Data
International T20I & ODI Ball-by-ball delivery records
Main finding
The stroke the batter plays largely decides how the wicket falls. The delivery matters mostly by choosing that stroke.

Shot type has a large association with both outcomes. Every bowling variable is small on its own, yet each still adds significant information once the stroke is known.

Shot typeV ≈ 0.5Large association with both outcomes
Each bowling variableV ≤ 0.16Small alone, still significant once the stroke is known
  • Short ball→Pulls and hooks
  • Full ball→Drives
  • Swing→Edges
  • Yorkers, cutters→Hit the stumps

Knowing the batter's likely stroke tells a captain far more about where the catch will go than knowing the bowler's type or arm.

What is linked to LBW vs Bowled?

How to read: same scale as the left chart. Select a bar to see LBW rates for each category.

The same pattern holds for a completely different outcome, which makes the stroke-first conclusion robust.
The stroke map · observed catches

Each stroke has a home catching zone

How to read: select a stroke for its fielding plan. Each row is 100% of the catches from that stroke, split by quadrant. Q1 = slips to third man, Q2 = cover to long off, Q3 = mid-wicket to long on, Q4 = fine leg to short leg (right-handed batter; mirrored for left-handers).

Cuts and defensive edges go behind square on the off side (74% Q1). Drives go to cover and mid off (60% Q2). Slogs, pulls and flicks go to mid-wicket and long on (62–67% Q3). Pulls, sweeps and flicks also feed fine leg and backward square (22–29% Q4).
Length · observed (n = 7,127; 9 yorkers omitted)

Length moves the catch

Short balls put 28% of catches at fine leg and backward square (2.5× the average). Half volleys put 41% through cover and mid off.
Variation · observed

Swing finds the slips

59% of catches off swinging or seaming balls are in Q1, almost three times the stock-ball rate. Slower balls and cutters push catches in front of square on the leg side.
Format effect

LBW is less common in T20Is

How to read: observed share of LBW among LBW + Bowled dismissals, and the model's adjusted share after holding stroke, line, length and variation fixed.

T20I dismissals have 28% lower odds of being LBW (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58–0.89), consistent with more aggressive, front-foot batting.
Why this research is valuable

What the study adds

  1. Delivery level, not match levelMost cricket models predict who wins; this one models the ball that takes the wicket.
  2. First four-zone catching modelEarlier fielding studies used binary outcomes such as catch vs drop.
  3. LBW contrasted with BowledModelled directly against each other, with match format tested as a factor.
  4. Imbalance handled openlyRecall, balanced accuracy, AUC and Brier score, plus weighted refits.
  5. Checked against machine learningXGBoost and random forest agree on the ranking of predictors.
  6. Directly usableFor field placements, bowling plans and DRS reviews.
catches by fielding position

Where catches are actually taken

Each dot is a named fielding position, sized by the number of catches taken there in T20I and ODI matches. Wicketkeeper and bowler catches are excluded.

Key insight

Catches cluster in a handful of places. The two boundary riders in front of square on the leg side, deep mid-wicket and long on, take almost a quarter of all catches. Add long off, mid off, slip and backward point and six positions take nearly half.

48.1%of all catches are taken at just six positions

Catching-zone model · multinomial logistic regression

Field Planner: if a catch comes, where will it go?

Describe the delivery and the stroke you expect. The model gives the probability of each catching quadrant. Those probabilities are then spread over the named positions in each quadrant using the observed catch shares per position, to rank where catchers matter most.

Key insight

Tell the planner what the bowler will bowl and what the batter is likely to play. The stroke does most of the work: drives go to cover and mid off (Q2), cuts and defensive edges to the slips and point (Q1), slogs and pulls to mid-wicket and long on (Q3), and sweeps to fine leg (Q4).

62.5%of unseen catches put in the right zone (40.9% by guessing)
Prediction · catching-zone model

Where a catch from this ball is likely to go

How to read: darker quadrant = more likely catching zone (outlined = most likely). Dot size = expected share of catches at that position.

Zone probabilitiesP(zone)
Catchers to prioritise for this ballExpected share

    Expected share = P(quadrant) × that position's share of catches within the quadrant. Assumes the within-quadrant mix is the same for every delivery.

    LBW or Bowled? Dismissal data vs all deliveries

    Set one delivery. Panel 1 gives the main result from dismissal data only. Panel 2 gives the result when every delivery is included. Panel 3 compares the two probabilities and conclusions. Panel 4 gives DRS review support from XGBoost, the model that misses the fewest LBWs.

    Go to step
    Key insight

    When a straight ball beats the bat, the stroke decides the result. Strokes played across or around the front pad (working, flicking, glancing, sweeping) end LBW; drives, cuts and slogs miss the ball and it hits the stumps. Yorkers, cutters and slower balls also favour Bowled.

    DRS review support · XGBoost

    LBW appeal on this ball: review or save it?

    XGBoost on the same 4,050 dismissals and the same 60/20/20 split, all eight factors · cut-off 0.189 chosen on validation data (Youden)

    Why XGBoost for DRS

    A review is lost for good when a real LBW is missed, so the DRS model should catch as many LBWs as possible. On the 809 unseen test dismissals XGBoost had the highest sensitivity, the best AUC and the best Brier score of the three models.

    Why XGBoost for DRS · test set, 809 dismissals (265 LBW)

    Which model misses the fewest LBWs?

    How to read: each model uses its own cut-off chosen on the validation set. Missed LBWs are the reviews a team would wrongly let go; false LBW flags are Bowled dismissals flagged as LBW.

    The model learns from completed LBW and Bowled dismissals; it does not track the ball. It says how LBW-prone this delivery and stroke are, so use it alongside the umpire's view and ball-tracking, not in place of them. XGBoost and the logistic model come from Lbw_Bowled_Train_Valid_Test_ML.Rmd; the XGBoost trees are re-fitted by analysis/xgboost_drs_model.R and reproduce the report exactly (cut-off 0.189, test matrix 330 / 22 / 214 / 243, AUC 0.846).

    Practical implications

    From odds ratios to match plans

    Start from the batter's favourite stroke. The table combines the observed catching zone, the busiest catching positions and the model's LBW chance.

    Key insight

    Read the batter first: their favourite stroke tells you where catches will go and whether a straight ball is more likely to trap them LBW or bowl them. Every plan below is backed by a statistically significant effect in the study models.

    7batter types with a ready-made field and bowling plan
    Batter profiles · 7 stroke types

    Batter profile quick guide

    Select a row for the full plan

    Straight-ball dismissal: the more likely of LBW or Bowled from the LBW vs Bowled model for an ODI, good length, off-side stock ball. LBW per ball: the all-deliveries model for the same ball from a pace bowler. Catching zone: most common quadrant for that stroke group.

    Field plans at a glance · 7 batter types

    Where to put the catchers for each batter

    How to read: each field is shaded by the share of that stroke group's catches in each quadrant (darker = more catches); the busiest zone is outlined and its main catching positions are numbered (names under each field). Right-handed batter. Select a field for the full plan.

    Field plan · Q1 · Q2

    Off-side catchers

    • ×4.45Swinging or seaming ball: odds of a slip, gully or point catch. Keep the slip cordon.
    • ×1.96Off-side line: Q1 odds ×1.96, Q2 ×1.55. Field the off side for off-side plans.
    • ×15.9Batter likely to drive: Q2 odds. Catchers at long off (510 catches), mid off (450) and extra cover (264).
    • 373Q1 hot spots: slip (373), backward point (369), short third man (242).
    Field plan · Q3 · Q4

    Leg-side catchers

    • ×14.2Sweep or scoop: Q4 odds. Fine leg and deep backward square are essential.
    • ×2.85Short-pitched pace: Q4 odds ×1.98 (short length) and ×2.85 (pace vs leg spin).
    • 930Q3 is the busiest zone: deep mid-wicket (930) and long on (803) take a quarter of all catches.
    • 0.43–0.59Slower balls, cutters and spin lower Q4 odds: bring fine leg up.
    Bowling plan

    Hunting LBW

    • ×17–28Target batters who work, flick, glance or sweep: LBW odds compared with a drive.
    • ×1.96Swing nearly doubles LBW odds. Bowl off-side or straight lines; a leg-side line cuts LBW odds by 30%.
    • −28%LBW is more common in ODIs: T20I odds are 28% lower.
    Bowling plan

    Hunting Bowled

    • −61%Yorkers cut LBW odds by 61%: the ball goes under the bat onto the stumps.
    • 0.41Cutters (OR 0.42) and changes of pace (OR 0.41) beat the batter through the gate.
    • StraightAgainst drivers, cutters and sloggers a straight ball is far more likely to bowl than trap.
    Decision support

    DRS reviews

    • > 50%Working, flicking, glancing and sweeping against full toss, good length and back of length: predicted LBW chance above 50%.
    • 76%Ranking dismissals by the model, the top 20% contain 43% of all LBWs and the top 40% contain 76%.
    • 91.7%XGBoost DRS model (LBW vs Bowled tab, panel 4) found 243 of 265 test LBWs. Below its 18.9% cut-off only 22 of 352 test dismissals were LBW: save the review.
    Limitations

    Read with care

    • DesignObservational data: associations, not causes. Shot type is itself a response to the delivery.
    • DataClustering by match, bowler and batter not modelled; no ball-tracking data; fielder placements not recorded.
    • SampleSmall cells (9 LBWs from cuts and steers, 21 glances, 9 yorker catches) give wide intervals.
    Held-out test sets

    Do the readable models hold up?

    Each question compared an interpretable regression with tree-based machine learning on the same data split. Machine learning gained almost nothing, so the regressions were kept because they also give odds ratios, confidence intervals and p-values.

    Key insight

    Yes, the models can be trusted. The simple regression models predict as well as machine learning (AUC 0.838 vs 0.841–0.846 for LBW; 0.808 vs 0.811 for catching zones) and they explain why. Every standard check passed. The only caution is that a few small groups, such as cuts and steers, have wide uncertainty.

    ≈ sameaccuracy as machine learning, with full explanations

    Data & Methodology

    From ball-by-ball data to two datasets

    Key insight

    International T20I and ODI ball-by-ball records were cleaned into two datasets: 7,136 catches with a known fielding position and 4,050 LBW or Bowled dismissals. Select any step, quadrant or bar below for details.

    Caught data7,136Caught; keeper, bowler and "no position" catches excluded
    LBW and Bowled data4,050Bowled 2,722 · LBW 1,328 (ODI 2,124 · T20I 1,926)

    Splits: the catching-zone model used 70/30 train/test; the LBW vs Bowled model used 60/20/20 train/validation/test, stratified, set.seed(123).
